section.title: The Woman in the Basket
section.sectionRationale: The seventh night vision completes the cleansing begun by the flying scroll. Wickedness itself, personified as a woman, is sealed inside a measuring basket under a lead weight and carried off to Shinar, the land of Babylon, to be housed there. Sin is not merely punished in individuals; it is removed bodily from the land and sent back to its home.
section.thesis: God does not only judge sinners under the curse; He removes the very principle of wickedness from among His people, sealing it up and deporting it to Babylon, so that the restored land may be holy for His dwelling.
section.frameNote: One movement: the measuring basket brought forward, Wickedness revealed and shut inside under a lead cover, and the two winged women carrying the basket to build it a house in the land of Shinar.

verses.text: Then the angel who was speaking with me came forward and told me, “Now lift up your eyes and see what is approaching.”
“What is it?” I asked. And he replied, “A measuring {{ephah|basket}} is going forth.” Then he continued, “This is their iniquity in all the land.”
And behold, the cover of lead was raised, and there was a woman sitting inside the basket.
“This is {{rishah|Wickedness}},” he said. And he shoved her down into the basket, pushing down the lead cover over its opening.
Then I lifted up my eyes and saw two women approaching, with the wind in their wings. Their wings were like those of a stork, and they lifted up the basket between heaven and earth.
“Where are they taking the basket?” I asked the angel who was speaking with me.
“To build a house for it in the land of {{shinar|Shinar}},” he told me. “And when it is ready, the basket will be set there on its pedestal.”

ephah.gloss: A dry measure of about twenty two liters, a standard commercial container used in the marketplace. Its appearance here, large enough to hold a seated woman, links wickedness to dishonest trade, the false measures and cheating in the market that the prophets so often condemned. The basket becomes the vessel in which sin is measured, sealed, and shipped away.

rishah.gloss: Wickedness, guilt, the settled condition of being in the wrong before God. The angel personifies it as a woman inside the basket, showing that God deals not only with individual sinful acts but with the very principle and power of evil at work among His people, which He removes bodily from the land.

shinar.gloss: Shinar, the ancient name for the plain of Babylonia, the site of Babel and its tower, the archetypal land of rebellion against God. Sending wickedness there to be given a house on a pedestal means returning evil to its spiritual home, where it will be enshrined and idolized, far from the cleansed land of God's people.

basic.context: This is the seventh night vision, and it pairs with the sixth. Where the flying scroll judged individual sinners, this vision removes wickedness itself. A commercial basket, an ephah, comes forward. Inside sits a woman the angel names Wickedness. He shoves her back down and seals the basket with a heavy lead lid. Then two winged women carry the basket off to Shinar, that is Babylon, to build it a house there. Sin is measured, sealed, and deported to its true home.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a symbolic vision, and its images are meant to be read together. The basket is a marketplace measure, tying wickedness to dishonest trade. The woman personifies evil as a power, not just a deed. The lead cover shows it firmly contained. The journey to Shinar shows sin returned to Babylon, the biblical home of rebellion, where it belongs. The point is a thorough, decisive cleansing of the land.
basic.originalLanguages: The container is an ephah, a standard dry measure from the market, hinting at the cheating and false weights the prophets condemned. The figure inside is rishah, wickedness itself personified. And the destination is Shinar, the plain of Babel and Babylon, the archetypal land of rebellion against God, where evil is given a house and a pedestal, enshrined at its own source.
basic.typology: The removal of wickedness from the land points forward to the final, complete removal of sin from God's people and God's world. Babylon as the home of evil anticipates the Babylon of Revelation, the great harlot city of rebellion, finally judged and thrown down so that the holy city can come.
basic.christ: This vision shows God's determination to take sin away, not merely to cover it over. That purpose is accomplished in Christ, the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world, who removes our transgressions as far as the east is from the west. What the vision pictures as sealing evil in a basket and shipping it to Babylon, the gospel accomplishes at the cross and will complete when Babylon falls forever.
basic.god: God is holy and thorough. He does not tolerate a little wickedness among His people; He measures it, seals it, and sends it away to its own place. He is sovereign even over evil, appointing where it goes and confining it under a weight it cannot lift. And He is committed to a clean dwelling, a land and a people fit for His holy presence.
basic.crossReferences: Revelation 17 and 18 show Babylon as the home of wickedness, finally judged. Micah 6 condemns the false measures of the marketplace. 1 John 3 says Christ appeared to take away sins. Psalm 103 says God removes our transgressions from us.
basic.oneStory: The cleansing of the land continues: wickedness itself is removed, sealed up, and sent home to Babylon. This anticipates the day when sin is taken away entirely and Babylon falls forever, so that the holy city and its cleansed people can dwell with God. The whole story bends toward a world with the wickedness finally deported and destroyed.

context.literary:
Zechariah received all eight night visions on a single night, dated in 1:7 to the twenty-fourth day of the eleventh month of Darius's second year. Many interpreters see the eight arranged as a mirror. The riders of the first vision answer the chariots of the eighth, the horns and craftsmen of the second answer the basket of the seventh, the man with the measuring line of the third answers the flying scroll of the sixth, and the two visions about Joshua and Zerubbabel stand together at the centre. On that plan the basket is not an afterthought. It is the counterpart of the vision about the four horns that scattered Judah: there the nations are cut down, here the corruption inside God's own land is carried out of it.

The vision is told in a tight sequence of seeing and asking. Zechariah lifts his eyes in 5:5 and again in 5:9, and twice he asks what he is looking at, in 5:6 and 5:10. The explanations are short and cryptic, and each one hands the next image to the reader. The angel who names the basket in 5:6, names its occupant in 5:8, and names its destination in 5:11 never explains why a woman or why a basket. The vision wants to be felt as a movement: something is revealed, pressed down, sealed, lifted and carried away.

It also pairs closely with the scroll of 5:1-4. The scroll goes out over the whole land and enters particular houses, the house of the thief and the house of the perjurer. The basket carries away what those houses were feeding. Chapter 5 therefore runs from the sin of persons to the system behind them, and 5:11 closes the chapter with the one word that turns the whole thing around: a house is being built. After two visions about removing, the text ends with something being constructed.
context.historical:
In 519 BC the community in Judah was a few tens of thousands of people under Persian rule, rebuilding on the ruins of a city the Babylonians had broken in 586. Scales, measures and weights were the daily stuff of the market, and the Law had always treated them as a matter of covenant faithfulness, Leviticus 19:35-36 and Deuteronomy 25:13-16. Amos had already lashed merchants who 'reduce the ephah and increase the shekel,' Amos 8:5, and Micah had named the 'short ephah' as accursed, Micah 6:10. Proverbs says plainly that dishonest scales are an abomination to the LORD, Proverbs 11:1. To a people hearing the angel say 'a measuring basket is going forth,' the first thing a market stall would bring to mind was a measure that had been cheated.

Shinar was an old name that carried weight. It was where Nimrod's kingdom began in Babylon, Genesis 10:10, and where the whole earth settled on the plain and built a city and a tower to make a name for themselves, Genesis 11:2-4. When Nebuchadnezzar took the temple vessels in 605 BC, Daniel 1:2 says he carried them to 'the land of Shinar, to the house of his god.' So the word did not simply mean Babylon as a map location. It meant the place where humanity organised itself against God, and where Judah's holy things had once been put in a rival temple's treasury. Many of the people Zechariah addressed had been born there, and the men named in 6:10 had just arrived from there. For them, hearing that wickedness was going to Shinar meant that the land of their long captivity would now take what had taken them.

Meanwhile the temple was half built. Haggai and Zechariah were urging the work along, and Ezra 6:14-15 records it was finished in Darius's sixth year. A holy house needs a clean land. The basket vision sits in that tension between a sanctuary going up and a community that still carried the habits that had sent it into exile.
context.canonical:
The vision draws on three long threads of Scripture. The first is the market thread, from the honest ephah of Leviticus 19:36 to the prophets who found the short ephah in Israel's markets, Amos 8:5 and Micah 6:10-11, to a New Testament in which the love of money is a root of every kind of evil and Revelation's merchants are 'the great ones of the earth,' Revelation 18:23. Wickedness in a measuring basket is one place where the Bible's worship of God and its economics meet.

The second is the Babel to Babylon thread. Shinar appears in Genesis 10:10 and 11:2, in Daniel 1:2 and here. The Bible's last Babylon is clearly modelled on its first. In Revelation 17:1-5 the great prostitute is seated in a wilderness, holding a golden cup, with a name written on her forehead, and Revelation 18:2 and 18:21 describe her fall, a stone cast into the sea 'never to be seen again.' The image in Zechariah of a woman called Wickedness taken to Shinar and set up in a house is not quoted by John, but the pieces are the same: a woman, a city of Shinar, an enshrined evil, and finally a removal that cannot be reversed.

The third thread is God dealing with sin by taking it away. Zechariah 3:4 shows Joshua's filthy clothes removed and his iniquity taken away. Zechariah 3:9 promises 'I will remove the iniquity of this land in a single day.' Chapter 5 shows the other half of that promise, the removal of the land's iniquity as an object carried out of the country. The New Testament names the one in whom both halves are completed, John 1:29 and Hebrews 9:26. Zechariah 13:1 completes the thought with a fountain opened 'to cleanse them from sin and impurity.'

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Zechariah wanted a discouraged, half-hearted community to take two things to heart. The first is that God treats sin as a power as well as a list of deeds. The scroll dealt with the thief and the liar by name; the basket deals with what makes thieves and liars. Restored Judah could not hope to keep the land clean simply by catching offenders. The root had to be removed, and only God can do that.

The second is that this removal is accomplished, not merely hoped for. The verbs run in a row: the cover is raised, she is pushed down, the lid is pressed on, the basket is lifted and carried. The angel is entirely in control of the woman, and her struggle is over in a single verse. A community who feared the corruption of its own city could hear this as comfort. Zechariah also meant the hearers to see that the sin sent away had a home to be sent to. The people who had come out of Babylon were being told that what they had fled would not follow them back.

The vision also quietly asks for a response. The chapter just before it speaks of a curse that lands on dishonesty. The hearers are being invited to stand on the side of the angel and not the basket, to let go of crooked scales before they are sealed up with them.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
This is a vision, and visions describe what God is doing without telling the reader how to do it. Nothing in the passage commands anyone to build a basket, to measure sin or to send it anywhere. The text does not ask the community to deport wicked people either; the figure being carried off is an image of evil, not a picture of a human group. Reading it as a charter for expelling people would turn a picture of God's work against the very people he came to save.

What it prescribes by implication is a posture. God is the one who removes sin, so the people of God are to bring their sin to him and not to hide it in the market or defend it at home. The practical hearing of the vision is therefore close to the hearing of the Law it lies near: keep honest scales, because the God who judges dishonesty has also promised to clear it away. The enduring truths are that evil is contained and answerable, that God owns the removal of it, and that his people are expected to live as those from whom it has been taken.

debates.question: Why is the figure a woman, and what does her gender mean?

views.label: A grammatical personification
views.case: The Hebrew noun for wickedness, rishah, is feminine, so a woman is the natural way to picture it. The same pattern appears in Proverbs, where wisdom and folly are both women. On this reading the text makes no comment about women at all, and it simply gives an abstract noun a body so that the angel can handle it.

views.label: A forerunner of the harlot of Babylon
views.case: The woman is carried by winged women to a house in Shinar, and Revelation later shows a woman named Babylon the Great, enthroned in a city of rebellion, Revelation 17:5. Those who read the two together see wickedness here as an idolatrous seduction, the false religion at the heart of Babylon, not only a market habit.

debates.bearing: Neither reading makes the text a judgment on women. It uses a grammatical gender and a long biblical habit of personifying cities and powers. The safest reading takes the image as a personification of evil as a power, and treats the Revelation link as a later echo of a pattern, not as a claim Zechariah himself made.

debates.question: What does 'This is their iniquity' mean in 5:6?

views.label: Iniquity, with the BSB
views.case: The BSB follows one Hebrew manuscript, the Septuagint and the Syriac, which read 'iniquity.' The basket then stands for the sum of sins, and the next verses name the woman inside it as Wickedness. The reading fits the movement from the scroll's guilty persons to evil itself.

views.label: 'Their appearance' or 'their eye,' with most Hebrew manuscripts
views.case: Most Hebrew manuscripts read what the footnote gives as 'their appearance' or, literally, 'their eye.' The sense would be 'this is what they look like throughout the land,' the visible face of the nation's corruption, or the way the people view things. It is a smaller change in the letters than it looks, and it keeps the angel's remark close to the picture.

debates.bearing: Both readings have the angel identify the basket with the land's moral condition. The choice affects whether the text speaks directly of iniquity or of its visible face, but not what happens to it. The BSB reading is the most widely followed.

debates.question: Who are the two women with stork wings?

views.label: Angelic agents of God
views.case: They are borne by the wind and lift the basket 'between heaven and earth,' the same medium God uses elsewhere to carry out his will. Their wings and their errand suit the heavenly messengers of the next vision, who are called the four spirits or winds of heaven, Zechariah 6:5. The stork is an unclean bird in Leviticus 11:19, which some take as fitting for carrying impurity away.

views.label: Agents or accomplices of wickedness
views.case: The text does not call them angels, as it does the interpreting angel, and the unclean stork might suggest they belong to the evil they carry. Women carrying a woman to a house in Shinar may mean wickedness has its own helpers. Those who take this line often connect them to the false religion Babylon embodies.

debates.bearing: The text does not tell us, and the point of the vision does not depend on it. What matters is that the basket moves where it is sent and arrives where the angel says. Whoever the carriers are, they serve the purpose declared in 5:11.

study.originalLanguages:
The word for the container is ephah, and it matters that it is a measure first and a basket second. The picture is of a standard unit of trade being brought out. In Leviticus 19:36 God demands 'an honest ephah.' Micah 6:10 calls the 'short ephah' accursed. Amos 8:5 pictures merchants who 'reduce the ephah.' The vessel that carries the woman is therefore the very thing the Law said must be true. Its use here is a pointed irony: the measure used to cheat the poor now measures out the sin that cheated them.

The woman is rishah, a feminine noun from the root rasha, which means to be guilty or wicked. It is not the common word for a sinful deed; it is the abstract state, wickedness as such. In the Psalms and Proverbs the rasha is the wicked person, set against the righteous. Here the quality itself is given a body and seated 'in the midst of the ephah.' The angel pushes her back down in 5:8 and presses the lead over the opening, and the cover in 5:7 is a kikkar, a round disc, here of lead. Lead is the heaviest of the common metals, a fitting seal for something that must not get out. The cover is lifted only long enough for her to be seen, and then it is closed.

Verse 6 contains a textual puzzle. Where the BSB reads 'This is their iniquity,' most Hebrew manuscripts read ayin, 'eye' or 'appearance,' with a pronoun, 'their eye.' The BSB footnote notes that one Hebrew manuscript, the Septuagint and the Syriac read 'iniquity,' which is the form awonam and differs from 'their eye' by a single letter. Either way the angel is describing the condition of the whole land, not one house.

The winged women are carried by 'the wind in their wings,' and the word for wind is ruach, the same word Zechariah will hear in the next vision, where the angel names four chariots as 'the four spirits of heaven,' with a footnote that it may also mean winds, 6:5. The word covers wind, breath and spirit, and the prophet lets the reader move between them. The wings are compared to a stork's, and Leviticus 11:19 lists the stork among the unclean birds, which may be why these carriers are fitted to bear an unclean cargo.

Finally, the building verb. In 5:11 the angel says the women go 'to build a house for it,' livnot lah bayit, using the ordinary words for building and for a house, and that is also what the temple is called throughout the prophecy, 'the house of the LORD.' The vocabulary is chosen so that two buildings stand across the prophecy from one another. Zechariah 1:16, 4:9 and 6:12-15 describe the house God's people build; 5:11 describes the house wickedness is given, a counter-temple in the land of rebellion.

typology.fulfillment: Wickedness sealed in a vessel and carried out of the land is a picture of sin dealt with by God's own hand. The correspondence in Christ is the lifting of sin from the people and its removal. John calls him 'the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world,' John 1:29, and Hebrews 9:26 says he appeared 'to do away with sin by the sacrifice of Himself.' The escalation is that the vision removes sin from a place, while Christ removes it from persons, by bearing it. The type falls short because the basket only relocates sin to Shinar. Christ puts sin to death in his own body, and a deported evil still exists, whereas a forgiven one is gone, Hebrews 10:12-14.

typology.type: The land of Shinar as the house of rebellion
typology.fulfillment: The plain where humanity first built a tower in defiance of God becomes in Scripture the place wickedness is at home. It reaches its last form in Revelation's Babylon, 'the mother of prostitutes,' who falls with the cry 'Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great,' Revelation 18:2, and is thrown down 'never to be seen again,' 18:21. The escalation is that what Zechariah shows as a removal becomes in John a public judgment, with the whole world watching. The type falls short in that Babylon in Zechariah is a real city and in John is a symbol for a worldwide system, so the pattern is not a one-to-one map. God's people are told in Revelation 18:4 to 'come out of her,' which is the vision's practical echo for the church.

typology.type: A house built for evil against a house built for God
typology.fulfillment: The vision sets two buildings side by side without saying so. God's house rises in Jerusalem, while a house for wickedness is built in Shinar. In the New Testament the true house is not stone but people, 'you also, like living stones, are being built into a spiritual house,' 1 Peter 2:5, and Christ says he himself will raise the temple, John 2:19-21. The counter-house is the world system that sets itself against his. The escalation is that the two houses become two cities, the New Jerusalem and Babylon, with no temple in the one because 'the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple,' Revelation 21:22. It is a type only by contrast, and it falls short in that Zechariah never calls the house in Shinar a temple. That language is inferred.

study.christ:
The vision does not name a deliverer, and it is wise not to force one into it. There is no figure here to identify with Jesus: the angel is not the Messiah, and the women are not saviours. What the vision does is state in picture form the problem that Christ comes to solve and the manner in which God solves it. Sin is not merely a debt to be paid; it is a power that has to be removed, and the one who removes it is stronger than it. The angel who casts down the woman and closes the lid is the kind of authority the New Testament gives to Christ over every power that holds people captive, Colossians 2:15.

The nearest link to Christ comes through the surrounding visions and not through the text itself. Zechariah 3:8-9 says God will bring his servant the Branch and 'remove the iniquity of this land in a single day.' In 6:12-13 the Branch builds the temple and sits as priest on his throne. Chapter 5 shows what the removal looks like from the side of sin; the other chapters show who does it. When John the Baptist points to Jesus and cries 'Look, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!', John 1:29, the claim is that the single day of Zechariah 3:9 has come. Hebrews 9:26 gives the answer in plain prose: he has 'appeared once for all at the end of the ages to do away with sin by the sacrifice of Himself.'

A second link is the contrast of two houses. A house is built in Shinar so that evil may sit there on its pedestal. Jesus says, 'Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up again,' and John explains that he was speaking of the temple of his body, John 2:19-21. The place where God dwells with his people is no longer a building to be guarded from a wicked woman in a basket. It is a person who bore sin, was laid in a tomb and rose. The result is that the new dwelling cannot be compromised the way the first temple was.

The vision also teaches by contrast with what Jesus did not do. The basket removes sin by sending it away, a scapegoat idea like the one on the Day of Atonement, Leviticus 16:21-22. Jesus did not send our sin to a far country. He carried it, 1 Peter 2:24, and in dying he met the wages of it, Romans 6:23. Zechariah gives a picture of the outcome, a land with its wickedness gone. The gospel gives the means, a substitute who stood where the guilty would have stood.

Finally, the vision guards against a cheap view of the cross. The woman is sealed with lead because sin is serious and cannot be waved away. If God had thought lightly of wickedness he would have needed no lid. The sheer weight of the metal is a measure of the cost that Christ paid. That is not forced allegory; it is the plain implication of a God who removes sin rather than ignoring it.
study.god:
The first thing this vision shows is that God is sovereign over evil. The woman is not a rival deity. She is a creature in a basket, and the angel who speaks with Zechariah controls her with a hand and a lid. She does not argue, she does not escape, and she does not choose where she goes. That is a necessary corrective to any picture in which wickedness is an equal and opposite power. The Bible holds that evil is real, dangerous and personal, but never co-ordinate with God. Even its destination is set by his word: 'to build a house for it in the land of Shinar.'

The second is God's holiness as an active, cleansing force. In many religions the holy is simply what is set apart; here it is what removes. God does not merely stay away from wickedness, he sends someone to take it out of the land where he intends to dwell. This fits the theme of the whole book, that God returns to Zion to live among his people, Zechariah 2:10-11 and 8:3. His presence will not coexist with the sin that drove him out. That is why the visions of cleansing, Joshua's clean garments, the scroll and the basket, come before the promise of his house.

Third, God cares about what happens in markets. The container is a measuring basket, and the prophets' complaint about the short ephah is a complaint about God's own character as truthful, Micah 6:10-11. A God who hates false weights is a God whose concern reaches into the small, daily dealings of ordinary people, the ones that rarely make a headline. Worship that ignores the scale in the shop is worship of a smaller god than the one Zechariah served. This matters directly in the next chapter, where the same prophet shows that hollow ritual is rejected when justice is neglected, Zechariah 7:5-10.

Fourth, God is patient and thorough at once. The same chapter that opens with a flying scroll of curse closes with a woman sealed away, and both belong to the same people's good. He does not leave a cleaned house empty. Chapter 6 immediately sends the chariots out to the whole earth and then crowns the Branch who will build the temple. The God of this vision is therefore not only the one who judges but the one who prepares. His removal of evil is the first half of his work of building.

For worship, the vision tells us what to confess. We do not need to hide sin from God, because he knows exactly where it is in the basket. We do not need to fear that sin will win, because its lid is lead and its destination is fixed. And we are not left to clean the land ourselves: the angel does it, and the people who bring honest scales to the market do so in gratitude, not in an attempt to earn a clean land.

crossReferences.note: The Law's command to keep honest scales and 'an honest ephah.' The vision uses the very measure the Law said must be true to carry away wickedness, so the basket speaks in the vocabulary of covenant honesty from Sinai.

Merchants who long for the Sabbath to end so they can 'reduce the ephah and increase the shekel' and 'cheat with dishonest scales.' Amos shows the market sin that Zechariah's ephah recalls, and shows that it was joined to trampling the poor, which is why wickedness belongs in a trader's basket.

Micah names 'the short ephah, which is accursed' among the treasures of wickedness. The ephah has been a symbol of Israel's economic injustice for centuries before Zechariah, and here God finally gathers it up and sends it out.

The plain of Shinar where people said 'let us build for ourselves a city with a tower.' When the angel says wickedness will have a house in Shinar, the hearer is meant to think of Babel, the first and defining counter-project to God's purpose.

Nebuchadnezzar carried the temple vessels to 'the land of Shinar, to the house of his god.' The vision answers that act: what Babylon did to Judah's holy things is reversed, and Judah's sin is carried back to Babylon's house.

Joshua's filthy clothes are removed with the words 'I have removed your iniquity,' and God promises to remove the land's iniquity in a single day. Chapter 5 shows that promise in action as a woman sealed and carried out of the land.

A woman with a mysterious name on her forehead, enthroned in a wilderness city of abomination. John does not quote Zechariah, but the figure of an evil woman tied to Babylon makes the vision the early form of what Revelation unfolds at full scale.
'Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great!' The outcome the basket points to arrives. The place where wickedness had its house becomes a lair for demons, so the pedestal in Shinar is finally brought down.

'Come out of her, My people, so that you will not share in her sins.' The practical call that follows the fall of Babylon is the reverse of the vision's exile of evil: God removes wickedness from his people, and his people are to leave its house.

John the Baptist points to Jesus as 'the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world.' What Zechariah sees as a removal of sin from the land is accomplished at the cross in a deeper way, by the removal of sin from persons.

Christ 'appeared once for all at the end of the ages to do away with sin by the sacrifice of Himself.' The vision's confident finality, the lid shut and the basket gone, is fulfilled in this once for all work.

study.oneStory:
The vision answers a question that begins in Genesis and does not stop until Revelation: what will God do with the evil that humanity built into the world? Genesis 3 brought sin in, Genesis 6:5 saw it saturate the human heart, and Genesis 11 saw it organised into a city on the plain of Shinar. Zechariah sees that organised evil taken out of God's land, carried back to Shinar, and set in a house of its own. The great story is thereby shown a decisive turning, in which wickedness becomes a thing God moves rather than a thing that moves God's people.

After the exile, though, evil did not vanish from Judah. Later prophets and the Gospels show the market, the temple courts and the throne still full of dishonesty. So the vision cannot be read as a plan for an immediate sinless nation. It is a promise whose first instalment is the cleansing of the temple community and whose fullness waits for a larger cleansing. Zechariah himself looks forward to a day when 'a fountain will be opened to the house of David and the people of Jerusalem, to cleanse them from sin and impurity,' Zechariah 13:1, and to a day when 'the LORD will become King over all the earth,' 14:9.

The gospel takes up the promise by putting the removal of sin on a person. The Lamb of God takes away the sin of the world, John 1:29, and by one offering makes perfect for all time those who are being sanctified, Hebrews 10:14. The church, as God's new house, is built from people who have been washed and set free, 1 Corinthians 6:11 and 1 Peter 2:5. Meanwhile the old pattern of Shinar continues in the world's systems, and the New Testament calls believers to come out of it, Revelation 18:4.

The story ends where the vision points. Babylon is thrown down and cannot be found again, Revelation 18:21. The city that replaces it has gates that never close, but 'nothing unclean will ever enter it,' Revelation 21:25-27, and the curse is gone, Revelation 22:3. There the basket and the pedestal are not needed, because the sin that required them has no place left. What Zechariah saw as a sealed lid and a distant house becomes a world in which wickedness is not merely contained but ended, and the temple is God himself with the Lamb.

quiz.q: What does the woman in the basket represent?

options.text: Wickedness itself, personified and removed from the land.
options.note: The angel names her This is Wickedness.

options.text: A particular sinful woman being judged.
options.note: She personifies wickedness as a power, not one individual.

options.text: The nation of Israel going into exile.
options.note: The vision removes wickedness, not the people, from the land.

options.text: A goddess the people should worship.
options.note: She is evil to be expelled, not a deity to be honored.

quiz.q: Where is the basket carried, and why?

options.text: To Shinar, that is Babylon, the home of rebellion, to be enshrined there.
options.note: Wickedness is returned to Babylon, its spiritual home, and given a house.

options.text: To Jerusalem, to be kept in the temple.
options.note: The opposite: it is removed far from the holy land, not kept in it.

options.text: To Egypt, to be destroyed at once.
options.note: It goes to Shinar, and is housed rather than immediately destroyed.

options.text: Nowhere; the basket stays in the land.
options.note: The whole point is that wickedness is carried away from the land.

quiz.q: How does this vision relate to the flying scroll before it?

options.text: Together they cleanse the land, one judging sinners, the other removing wickedness itself.
options.note: The pair prepares the land for God's holy presence.

options.text: They contradict each other.
options.note: They complement each other as a matched pair of cleansing visions.

options.text: They have nothing to do with each other.
options.note: They are deliberately paired to complete the theme of cleansing.

options.text: Both are about rebuilding the temple walls.
options.note: Both are about moral cleansing, not construction.

quiz.q: What does the marketplace basket suggest about the wickedness in view?

options.text: It is tied to dishonest trade and false measures.
options.note: The ephah is a commercial measure, linking wickedness to cheating in the market.

options.text: It is only about religious ritual.
options.note: The container points specifically to commerce, though sin is broader.

options.text: It has nothing to do with everyday life.
options.note: The market basket roots wickedness in ordinary economic dealings.

options.text: It shows the people were too poor to sin.
options.note: The basket exposes sin in trade, not poverty as innocence.

quiz.q: How does the vision point to Christ and the gospel?

options.text: God's purpose to take sin away is fulfilled in Christ, who bears it away for His people.
options.note: The Lamb of God takes away the sin of the world, John 1:29.

options.text: It shows sin can never really be removed.
options.note: The opposite: it shows God decisively removing wickedness.

options.text: It teaches we must carry our own sin to Babylon.
options.note: God removes the sin; we cannot deport our own guilt.

options.text: It has no gospel meaning.
options.note: It anticipates Christ taking away the sin of the world.

questions: God removes wickedness rather than tolerating it among His people. Where are you tempted to manage a sin rather than let God take it away?
The basket tied wickedness to the marketplace. How honest are you in your work, your money, and your dealings when no one is watching?
Wickedness was sent back to Babylon, its true home. What sinful pattern in your life needs to be sent away rather than given a house?
Christ takes away the sin of the world. How does it comfort you that God bears your guilt away rather than merely covering it over?
God is preparing a clean land for His presence. What would it look like this week to cooperate with His cleansing work in you?

translationNotes.note: Measuring basket renders ephah, a dry measure of about twenty two liters; a footnote in many editions notes the literal An ephah, tying the image to commerce and false measures.

This is their iniquity follows the reading of one Hebrew manuscript, the Septuagint, and Syriac; most Hebrew manuscripts read their appearance or literally their eye, a minor textual variant that does not change the sense of judgment on sin.
Shinar is the ancient name for Babylonia, the plain of Babel; building a house on a pedestal uses temple language, picturing wickedness enshrined in a false sanctuary at its own home.
